text:
Sasha: quick follow-up from the allocator rfc thread — i'm worried our current evictor admission API leaks scheduling decisions into the allocator. we need a clearer boundary so allocators can be pluggable without embedding tenant policies.

Mike: agreed. main tradeoff i see is: minimal API (evict this range / give me a victim) vs. policy-rich API (priority, cost hints, deadline). minimal keeps allocators simple but pushes complexity to caller.

Renee: what about an admission token model? caller requests an admission token with policy metadata, runtime returns token or wait handle. allocator just consumes tokens and reports back when done. that isolates policy logic.

Jorge: sketch of a small prototype API i hacked together:

```
// admission API (sync/async)
struct AdmissionRequest {
  tenant_id: String,
  bytes: usize,
  priority: u8, // 0..255, higher == more urgent
  deadline_ms: Option<u64>,
  prefer_cold: bool,
}

enum AdmissionResult {
  Granted(AdmissionToken),
  Queued(WaitHandle),
  Rejected,
}

// allocator only sees tokens:
struct AdmissionToken {
  id: u64,
  reclaimed_ranges: Vec<Range>,
}
```

Jorge: idea is runtime makes scheduling decisions and returns tokens. allocator doesn't need tenant policy details.

Sasha: i like token approach. couple questions: 1) do we let allocator fail token consumption (e.g., can't free enough) and hand back partial reclaim? 2) how do we account for observed reclaim slippage (allocator freed less than told) so runtime doesn't double-count capacity?

Mike: for (1) we should allow a TokenResult with metadata: {consumed_bytes, remaining_bytes, recycled}. runtime needs a reconciliation path: periodic reconciliation RPC where allocator reports actual freed counts.

Renee: also add a hint field for fragmentation sensitivity: `frag_sensitive: bool` so allocator can prefer coalescing or compacting vs. eager eviction. compacting is expensive but better for long-lived allocations.

Jorge: small tweak — make tokens lease-based with expiry to avoid stuck tokens if allocator crashes: token.expiry_ts and a reclaim callback from runtime if expired.

infra-bot: deploy scheduled: evictor-admission-proto v0.1 -> staging at 2026-03-21T14:00Z :rocket:

Sasha: sounds good. next: tenant fairness and burst smoothing. i think the runtime should enforce burst windows (tokens per epoch) and allocator should expose a fast-path that doesn't require tokens for tiny allocations (to keep latency).

Mike: tiny-alloc fast-path must still be accounted for — maybe local per-allocator reservoir that's periodically reconciled. keep it small (e.g., 32KB) to avoid abuse.

Renee: question on metrics: we need token latency histograms, token rejection rates, per-tenant reclaimed_vs_requested. add a label for `policy_source` (route/dedicated/private) so we can correlate regressions.

Jorge: i'll push the proto + a simulation harness that replays traces and applies different token budgets per tenant. can we sync tomorrow 9:30 to run it together?

Sasha: yes. add a short README with expected metrics and an opt-in flag in staging. want to see fragmentation / latency tradeoffs in real traces.

Mike: one last note — ensure the token format is compact and suitable for cross-process IPC (u64 ids, small bitflags). we don't want per-request JSON overhead at hot path.

Renee: ack. i'll draft a follow-up RFC section on observability and reconciliation rules.

Sasha: thanks all. i'll open a follow-up PR referencing jorge's proto and renee's metrics section. :thumbsup:
